rules_text:
Rules summary Gameplay Players take turns to play a tile to the table. Whenever you complete a closed network of paths of your colour (pink/yellow), place a stone on every house of your colour that's connected to that network. First to place all of their stones wins. If all tiles have been placed and no one has placed all of their stones, the player who placed more stones wins. Readability tip If you try to complete a path, but when you lay down a tile, it doesn't complete, look for other exits for the path. Four-way crossroads that don't have an underpass will extend your roads.

---

Life isn't easy in the enchanted forest. Elves and gnomes each have their own network of hidden paths. They don't want to be disturbed and will move into their houses only once they're protected from outsiders. Will you find your way or be lost in the forest?

In Fairy Trails, players play cards that expand the road network. Once a road is completed, that player may place a stone on each of their houses that are bordering that road. The player who places all their houses first wins.

—description from the publisher

[Rating: 1/10] A simple abstract race game about closing off connections and keeping your opponent's trails open.  The graphic design whilst pretty unfortunately makes it very difficult to track which trails are open or closed which is the raison d'être of the game.

[Rating: 1/10] Hated this. You need to be able to think ahead. I couldn’t make much sense of it. Wouldn’t play again.

[Rating: 2/10] This game is an inferior Carcassonne in every way.  It's very hard to determine what's going on.

[Rating: 2/10] It's a game about paths, where the paths are illegible and impossible to see.  Truly a graphic design tragedy, though I think even without that the underlying game is too long and too bland.

[Rating: 2/10] Despite the hand giving you a bit more room to maneuver (definitely would be worse if you were just drawing 1 tile like Carc) it still ended up feeling almost strategy-free. Interference only seemed relevant when I was 1 tile away from winning and couldn't draw it, so spent tiles "helping" my opponent, but I don't think that impacted the outcome at all really. Generally felt like there was an obvious best move every turn.  Despite having lots of options (in theory) of where to place tiles, in the end it felt like the game was entirely decided by luck. Art is pretty though.

[Rating: 2/10] Tile-laying throwback with an uninteresting push/close dilemma, not helped by the two-tile hand size putting a lot of weight onto the luck of the draw, and pretty much killed by the noodly organic card design that makes it easy to misread the gamestate.

[Rating: 3/10] Tile laying game that asks you to build a ton and hope you draw the right cards to outspeed the opponent.

[Rating: 3/10] This is one of the most boring games I’ve ever played. I didn’t care about a single turn. The only reason to play well was so the game would end sooner.

[Rating: 3/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  It doesn't really do much for me and the graphic design makes playing even more challenging to decipher the trails - which is a significant impediment when the key to the game is setting yourself up to close off trails of your color. I've played once on BGA two player and have no interest playing it solo as a puzzle.

[Rating: 3/10] The cards are hard to parse and the game just feels bereft of interesting choices. Not for me, although I wanted it to be.
